ethics_check.title: Ethics Approval Check
ethics_check.summary_text: 1 of 1 paper appeared to involve live data collection and lacked an ethics approval statement.

table.text: All participants provided informed consent and received financial compensation.
Primary English-speaking U.S. residents were recruited, targeting at least 30 participants per stimulus (Hehman et al., 2018; Stolier et al., 2018) and oversampling to account for exclusions.
table.formatted: Primary English-speaking U.S. residents were recruited, targeting at least 30 participants per stimulus <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Hehman et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Stolier et al., 2018)</ref> and oversampling to account for exclusions.

table.text: A total of 150 participants were recruited via Prolific (Mage = 41.31, SDage = 14.50; two implausible age responses excluded; 93 females, 56 males, 1 another gender; 113 White, 17 Black, 5 Asian, 10 Multiracial, 5 another race).
Participants were randomly assigned to evaluate a subset of 360 stimuli comprising 20 male and 20 female images in each of the three cropping conditions (full-face, face-without-eyes, eyes-only).

Before beginning, participants were informed that they would view images of faces or eyes displaying different mental state expressions and were instructed to identify the depicted mental state ("What is this person's mental state experience?").

Follow-up pairwise comparisons with Holm correction showed that participants were significantly more accurate in identifying mental states when viewing full faces than when viewing eyes-only, t(149) = 14.19, p < .001, or faces-without-eyes, t(149) = 8.27, p < .001.
table.formatted: Follow-up pairwise comparisons with Holm correction showed that participants were significantly more accurate in identifying mental states when viewing full faces than when viewing eyes-only, t(149) = 14.19, p < .001, or faces-without-eyes, t(149) = 8.27, p < .001.

table.text: A total of 451 participants were recruited via Amazon Mechanical Turk.
Each participant completed a face similarity judgment task followed by a conceptual association task.
We recruited 221 participants from Prolific.
Participants completed 10 practice trials, each randomly drawing from the 15 mental states in their assigned subset.
Thus, participants completed 30 face-judgment trials.
Following the face judgments task, participants completed a conceptual association task similar to the one used in Study 2.
Trial order and the left-right ordering of the two states within each trial were randomized.

Mental state pairs believed to be more likely to co-occur were more frequently confused in face judgments, and participants were more likely to select a particular incorrect state when they viewed it as more strongly associated with the depicted state, even after accounting for shared associations.
Because the study included two versions with different stimuli, we recruited a total of 102 participants through Prolific.
Because this set was too large for a single session, we randomly divided the stimuli into two subsets of 75 faces (five per state), and participants were assigned to one version.
When two states were more conceptually related, participants were more likely to confuse those states when judging naturalistic facial expressions.

Thus, even for naturalistic, unposed faces, participants were more likely to make a particular confusion when they personally viewed the depicted and selected states as more strongly associated than other participants did.
In Study 1, participants were more accurate in identifying mental states from full faces than from partial faces or isolated eye regions.

Studies 3 and 4 extended this relationship to specific mental state confusions: participants were more likely to misidentify a depicted state as another state when the two were more strongly conceptually associated.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.
We examined 168 columns across 25 data files.
#### Issues Identified
10 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(File = c("data_demo.csv", "s1_eyes.csv", "s1_eyes.csv", "s1_eyes.csv", "s1_full_face.csv", "s1_full_face.csv", "s1_full_face.csv", "s1_half_face.csv", "s1_half_face.csv", "s1_half_face.csv"), Column = c("...10", "Spreadsheet: answer", "Spreadsheet: display", "Spreadsheet: pics", "Spreadsheet: answer", "Spreadsheet: display", "Spreadsheet: pics", "Spreadsheet: answer", "Spreadsheet: display", "Spreadsheet: pics"), Issues = c("⬜ Empty column — Column is empty: all 451 values are missing", "🏷️ Problematic column name — Column name has characters not allowed in file names (\":\")", "🏷️ Problematic column name — Column name has characters not allowed in file names (\":\")", "🏷️ Problematic column name — Column name has characters not allowed in file names (\":\")", "🏷️ Problematic column name — Column name has characters not allowed in file names (\":\")", "🏷️ Problematic column name — Column name has characters not allowed in file names (\":\")", "🏷️ Problematic column name — Column name has characters not allowed in file names (\":\")", "🏷️ Problematic column name — Column name has characters not allowed in file names (\":\")", "🏷️ Problematic column name — Column name has characters not allowed in file names (\":\")", "🏷️ Problematic column name — Column name has characters not allowed in file names (\":\")" )), row.names = c(NA, -10L), class = "data.frame") # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 20, FALSE) ```
#### Careless Responding
No file could be screened for careless responding.

**What this does not cover.** Only 0 of 25 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

live_data_statements: All participants provided informed consent and received financial compensation.
Primary English-speaking U.S. residents were recruited, targeting at least 30 participants per stimulus (Hehman et al., 2018; Stolier et al., 2018) and oversampling to account for exclusions.

A total of 150 participants were recruited via Prolific (Mage = 41.31, SDage = 14.50; two implausible age responses excluded; 93 females, 56 males, 1 another gender; 113 White, 17 Black, 5 Asian, 10 Multiracial, 5 another race).
Participants were randomly assigned to evaluate a subset of 360 stimuli comprising 20 male and 20 female images in each of the three cropping conditions (full-face, face-without-eyes, eyes-only).

Before beginning, participants were informed that they would view images of faces or eyes displaying different mental state expressions and were instructed to identify the depicted mental state ("What is this person's mental state experience?").

Follow-up pairwise comparisons with Holm correction showed that participants were significantly more accurate in identifying mental states when viewing full faces than when viewing eyes-only, t(149) = 14.19, p < .001, or faces-without-eyes, t(149) = 8.27, p < .001.
A total of 451 participants were recruited via Amazon Mechanical Turk.
Each participant completed a face similarity judgment task followed by a conceptual association task.
We recruited 221 participants from Prolific.
Participants completed 10 practice trials, each randomly drawing from the 15 mental states in their assigned subset.
Thus, participants completed 30 face-judgment trials.
Following the face judgments task, participants completed a conceptual association task similar to the one used in Study 2.
Trial order and the left-right ordering of the two states within each trial were randomized.

Mental state pairs believed to be more likely to co-occur were more frequently confused in face judgments, and participants were more likely to select a particular incorrect state when they viewed it as more strongly associated with the depicted state, even after accounting for shared associations.
Because the study included two versions with different stimuli, we recruited a total of 102 participants through Prolific.
Because this set was too large for a single session, we randomly divided the stimuli into two subsets of 75 faces (five per state), and participants were assigned to one version.
When two states were more conceptually related, participants were more likely to confuse those states when judging naturalistic facial expressions.

Thus, even for naturalistic, unposed faces, participants were more likely to make a particular confusion when they personally viewed the depicted and selected states as more strongly associated than other participants did.
In Study 1, participants were more accurate in identifying mental states from full faces than from partial faces or isolated eye regions.

Studies 3 and 4 extended this relationship to specific mental state confusions: participants were more likely to misidentify a depicted state as another state when the two were more strongly conceptually associated.

report: This module assesses whether the paper's code could be run on its data, and — because `execute = TRUE` — **actually ran it**. We examined 5 R code files.
#### Run order
The scripts were ordered by their data dependencies (a script writing a file another reads runs first), `source()` calls, and numeric filename prefixes.
#### File paths

**18 data paths in the code do not work in the repository as deposited.** We pointed them to where the file is, so the code could run: `data_attn_v1.csv` to `S4/data/data_attn_v1.csv` (in Study4_analysis.R); `data_attn_v2.csv` to `S4/data/data_attn_v2.csv` (in Study4_analysis.R); `conceptual_long_v1.csv` to `S4/data/conceptual_long_v1.csv` (in Study4_analysis.R); `conceptual_long_v2.csv` to `S4/data/conceptual_long_v2.csv` (in Study4_analysis.R); `perceptual_long_v1.csv` to `S4/data/perceptual_long_v1.csv` (in Study4_analysis.R); `perceptual_long_v2.csv` to `S4/data/perceptual_long_v2.csv` (in Study4_analysis.R); `demos1.csv` to `S3/data/demos1.csv` (in Study3_analysis.R); `demos2.csv` to `S3/data/demos2.csv` (in Study3_analysis.R); `demos3.csv` to `S3/data/demos3.csv` (in Study3_analysis.R); `demos4.csv` to `S3/data/demos4.csv` (in Study3_analysis.R), and 8 more. The code should be changed, because as written it does not find these files.
#### Execution

**The code was run.** Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 5 scripts: 3 ran without error, 1 errored, 0 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions. **1 script needs the internet**, which is off during the run: Study1_analysis.R. Keeping what they download in the deposit solves this.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = c("Study1_analysis.R", "Study2_analysis.R", 
"Study3_analysis.R", "Study4_analysis.R", "Figure_combined_S3_S4.R"
), Outcome = c("needs_internet", "ran_ok", "ran_ok", "ran_ok", 
"errored"), Detail = c("", "", "", "", "runtime"), "Time (s)" = c(7.3, 
14.4, 22.4, 15.5, 2.9)), row.names = c(NA, -5L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 15, FALSE)
```
**`setwd()` in the code**

**2 scripts call `setwd()`.** This is bad practice: it hardcodes where the code must run (often an absolute path on the author's own machine) and breaks the moment the code is run anywhere else. To run the code we replaced these calls with a statement that does nothing. Any such script that then ran is **reproducible only after ignoring a `setwd()` that should not have been in the code and needs to be fixed**.
Reproducible after removing `setwd()`: Study4_analysis.R, Study3_analysis.R.

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list(File = c("Study4_analysis.R", "Study3_analysis.R"
), "setwd() removed" = c(1L, 1L), "Path(s) it set" = c("(non-literal)", 
"(non-literal)")), row.names = c(NA, -2L), class = "data.frame")

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, "auto", 10, FALSE)
```

info.title: CONCEPTUAL KNOWLEDGE STRUCTURES MENTAL STATE PERCEPTION

author.affiliation:
Department of Psychology
								New York University

text.text: The ability to infer others' mental states is central to understanding human behavior.
Across four studies (total N = 827), we examined how facial information and perceivers' conceptual knowledge structure mental-state inferences.

In Study 1, participants identified 60 complex mental states more accurately from full faces than from faces with the eye region removed or isolated eye regions, demonstrating the importance of information beyond the eyes.
Study 2 showed that mental states believed to co-occur were perceived as more similar in facial appearance.
Crucially, perceivers' idiosyncratic conceptual associations predicted their own facial-similarity judgments even after accounting for associations shared across participants.

Studies 3 and 4 extended this correspondence from perceptual similarity to categorical identification: conceptually associated states were more likely to be confused with one another, both for standardized posed expressions and for naturalistic, unposed faces.
On trials involving misidentification, participants' unique conceptual associations predicted which incorrect mentalstate label they selected above and beyond shared conceptual structure.
Together, these findings suggest that inferring mental states from faces depends on both distributed facial information and the conceptual organization perceivers bring to the task.
More broadly, they identify individual differences in conceptual knowledge as a source of systematic variation in how people read minds from the same facial expressions.

Statement of public significance: People often assume that understanding what someone is thinking or feeling is a matter of reading their facial expressions, especially their eyes, but our findings suggest that these judgments also depend on what observers believe about how different mental states relate to one another.

Across four studies, we found that facial information beyond the eyes helps people recognize complex mental states, while states believed to occur together tend to be perceived as more similar in facial appearance and are more likely to be confused with one another.

Importantly, individuals' unique beliefs about how mental states relate predicted their own perceptual judgments and specific errors beyond associations shared with others, even when viewing naturalistic faces, suggesting that two people looking at the same expression may interpret it differently partly because they bring different conceptual understandings of other minds to what they see.
Understanding others' thoughts, emotions, and intentions requires inferring mental states, a process known as mentalizing or mind-reading (Baron-Cohen et al., 2001).
text.formatted: Understanding others' thoughts, emotions, and intentions requires inferring mental states, a process known as mentalizing or mind-reading <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Baron-Cohen et al., 2001)</ref>.

text.text: Extensive work has explored the cognitive mechanisms underlying mental state inferences using explicit information (Barrett et al., 2011; Byom & Mutlu, 2013; Ho et al., 2022; Hudson et al., 2016; Mitchell, 2009; Saxe & Kanwisher, 2003).
text.formatted: Extensive work has explored the cognitive mechanisms underlying mental state inferences using explicit information <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Barrett et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">Byom & Mutlu, 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Ho et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Hudson et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Mitchell, 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">Saxe & Kanwisher, 2003)</ref>.

text.text: Far less clear, however, are the visual cues perceivers use to infer such states during social interactions.
For canonical emotions (e.g., joy, fear), decades of research show that people reliably distinguish emotional categories from facial expressions (Ekman, 1993; Ekman et al., 1987; Jack et al., 2016).
text.formatted: For canonical emotions (e.g., joy, fear), decades of research show that people reliably distinguish emotional categories from facial expressions <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Ekman, 1993;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Ekman et al., 1987;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Jack et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Recent work using naturalistic face-body expressions found that perceivers can distinguish 28 unique mental state dimensions (e.g., confusion, doubt, sympathy; Cowen & Keltner, 2020) 1 , yet the visual cues enabling such granular mental-state representations remain unclear.
text.formatted: Recent work using naturalistic face-body expressions found that perceivers can distinguish 28 unique mental state dimensions (e.g., confusion, doubt, sympathy; <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Cowen & Keltner, 2020)</ref> 1 , yet the visual cues enabling such granular mental-state representations remain unclear.

text.text: Much attention has focused on the role of the eyes in conveying mental states (Baron-Cohen et al., 2001; Lee & Anderson, 2017; Looser & Wheatley, 2010).
text.formatted: Much attention has focused on the role of the eyes in conveying mental states <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Baron-Cohen et al., 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Lee & Anderson, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Looser & Wheatley, 2010)</ref>.

text.text: The well-known Reading the Mind in the Eyes test demonstrates that observers can infer nuanced states such as suspicion or curiosity from the eye region alone, i.e., the eyes and eyebrows (Baron-Cohen et al., 2001).
text.formatted: The well-known Reading the Mind in the Eyes test demonstrates that observers can infer nuanced states such as suspicion or curiosity from the eye region alone, i.e., the eyes and eyebrows <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Baron-Cohen et al., 2001)</ref>.

text.text: The eyes convey not only strictly emotional states but also cognitively rich states like awe through cues such as gaze direction or eye-widening (Lee & Anderson, 2017).
text.formatted: The eyes convey not only strictly emotional states but also cognitively rich states like awe through cues such as gaze direction or eye-widening <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Lee & Anderson, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Yet the role of other facial features in mental-state perception remains unclear.

Although perceivers are sensitive to a wide range of facial cues, these have been studied primarily in the context of recognizing canonical emotional expressions (e.g., anger, joy; Dimberg et al., 2000; Ekman & Oster, 1979; Smith et al., 2005), and less is known about how they contribute to perceiving complex mental states (e.g., skepticism, curiosity).
text.formatted: Although perceivers are sensitive to a wide range of facial cues, these have been studied primarily in the context of recognizing canonical emotional expressions (e.g., anger, joy; <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Dimberg et al., 2000;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">Ekman & Oster, 1979;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Smith et al., 2005)</ref>, and less is known about how they contribute to perceiving complex mental states (e.g., skepticism, curiosity).

text.text: Research shows that people engage in holistic and configural processing of faces, such that individual features are perceived in relation to one another and to the face as a whole (Calder et al., 2000; Tanaka & Farah, 1993; Young et al., 1987).

text.text: While some studies suggest that mental-1 Throughout our work, we define mental states as internal, latent states, cognitive or affective, that occupy the mind without being overtly expressed.
This definition is intentionally broad and context-agnostic, encompassing moods and emotions as well as cognitive processes such as planning and reasoning (Thornton et al., 2023).

text.text: We propose that perceivers will be more accurate when viewing full faces because they integrate a broader set of cues.
Other expressive cues, such as those from the mouth, are important for nonverbal communication and may also contribute broadly to mental-state perception (Jack & Schyns, 2015; Wegrzyn et al., 2017).

text.text: Beyond visual cues themselves, contextual factors such as situational cues and prior conceptual knowledge contribute to the recognition of emotions and social categories (Barrett et al., 2011; Freeman & Ambady, 2011; Zaki et al., 2009), and are likely to influence mental state inferences.
text.formatted: Beyond visual cues themselves, contextual factors such as situational cues and prior conceptual knowledge contribute to the recognition of emotions and social categories <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Barrett et al., 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Freeman & Ambady, 2011;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Zaki et al., 2009)</ref>, and are likely to influence mental state inferences.

text.text: We propose that top-down conceptual knowledge, specifically, perceivers' understanding of how mental states relate to one another, plays a critical role in shaping mental state judgments.
For example, if confusion is conceptually related to skepticism in a perceiver's mind, that perceiver may rely on visually similar facial cues to perceive both states.
Such conceptual influences could shape the accuracy of these inferences.
In Study 1, we examined whether accuracy in detecting 60 unique mental states from faces is higher for full faces than partial facial cues.
Participants viewed images of either full faces, faces without the eye region, or the eye region alone, and selected the expressed mental state from four options.
We predicted that participants would be more accurate in judging mental states from full faces compared to cropped faces or eyes/eyebrows alone.
All participants provided informed consent and received financial compensation.
Primary English-speaking U.S. residents were recruited, targeting at least 30 participants per stimulus (Hehman et al., 2018; Stolier et al., 2018) and oversampling to account for exclusions.
text.formatted: Primary English-speaking U.S. residents were recruited, targeting at least 30 participants per stimulus <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Hehman et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Stolier et al., 2018)</ref> and oversampling to account for exclusions.

text.text: A total of 150 participants were recruited via Prolific (Mage = 41.31, SDage = 14.50; two implausible age responses excluded; 93 females, 56 males, 1 another gender; 113 White, 17 Black, 5 Asian, 10 Multiracial, 5 another race).
We selected 60 out of 93 mental states from the McGill Face Database (Schmidtmann et al., 2020).
text.formatted: We selected 60 out of 93 mental states from the McGill Face Database <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Schmidtmann et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: In the database, each mental state is portrayed by two actors (one male, one female).
Each actor had been instructed to portray every mental state, and their portrayals were validated by independent raters using a four-alternative forced-choice procedure.
The 60 mental states we selected were recognized above chance for both the male and female actor.
For each of the 120 images (60 male, 60 female), we generated two cropped versions: one isolating the eye region and one with the eye region removed.
Each of the 120 original faces thus appeared in three versions: full-face, face-without-eyes, or eyes-only (see Figure 1).
text.formatted: Each of the 120 original faces thus appeared in three versions: full-face, face-without-eyes, or eyes-only (see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_1">1</ref>).

text.text: For clarity, "eyes-only" denotes the cropped eyes-and-eyebrows region.
Participants were randomly assigned to evaluate a subset of 360 stimuli comprising 20 male and 20 female images in each of the three cropping conditions (full-face, face-without-eyes, eyes-only).

To ensure independence of ratings, if a participant saw a given mental state (e.g., "Sarcastic") for a given actor in one condition (e.g., female full-face), that stimulus was not presented again in the remaining conditions.
Across the three blocks, participants evaluated all 60 mental states twice each, once for a male face and once for a female face, with condition assignment randomized.
On average, each stimulus (actor × mental state × cropping condition) was rated by 50 participants.
On each trial, participants viewed a stimulus alongside four response options, one corresponding to the correct mental state.
The three foils were quasi-randomly selected from the remaining 59 mental states, and option order was randomized across participants.

Before beginning, participants were informed that they would view images of faces or eyes displaying different mental state expressions and were instructed to identify the depicted mental state ("What is this person's mental state experience?").
Ten attention checks were distributed across the three blocks.
Across all studies, participants who failed more than two were excluded.
No participants met this criterion in Study 1.
None of the studies were preregistered.

Average accuracy was calculated separately for each participant in the full-face, eyesonly, and face-without-eyes conditions.
One-sample t-tests confirmed that accuracy in detecting mental states was significantly above chance (25%) in all three conditions.

As expected, accuracy was above chance for the full-face condition (M = 65.27%, SD = 11.12%; t(149) = 44.33, p < .001, d = 3.62) and the eyes-only condition (M = 51.47%, SD = 11.05%; t(149) = 29.33, p < .001, d = 2.40), consistent with prior work (Baron-Cohen et al., 1997).

text.text: More importantly, participants also showed above-chance accuracy in the face-without-eyes condition (M = 57.33%, SD = 10.70%; t(149) = 37.02, p < .001, d = 3.02), indicating that cues outside the eye region support mental state recognition.

text.text: A repeated-measures ANOVA revealed significant differences in accuracy across conditions, F(2.00, 297.43) = 104.88, p < .001, ηp² = .41 (Figure 2).

text.text: Follow-up pairwise comparisons with Holm correction showed that participants were significantly more accurate in identifying mental states when viewing full faces than when viewing eyes-only, t(149) = 14.19, p < .001, or faces-without-eyes, t(149) = 8.27, p < .001.

text.text: Perhaps surprisingly, accuracy in the facewithout-eyes condition was also significantly higher than in the eyes-only condition, t(149) = 6.26, p < .001, highlighting the importance of cues beyond the eye region in facilitating mental state inferences.

In Study 1, we found above-chance accuracy in detecting 60 complex mental states from all facial feature conditions.
Cropped faces with the eye region removed not only elicited abovechance accuracy but permitted more accurate inferences than the eye region alone.

These findings extend previous research by highlighting that facial features beyond the eye region contribute to accurate mental state detection, suggesting that prior work may have underestimated their importance in mental state judgments.
Study 1 established that mental-state judgments draw on information distributed across the face.
Study 2 turned to how perceivers interpret that information, testing whether their conceptual knowledge of how mental states relate corresponds to the structure they perceive in facial expressions.
We predicted that states believed to co-occur would be perceived as perceptually more similar.
With 60 mental states, there are 1,770 unique pairs (e.g., perplexed and suspicious).
Following prior work with similar designs (Bin Meshar et al., 2022; Hehman et al., 2018; Stolier et al., 2018), we aimed to collect ratings from ~30 participants per pair.
text.formatted: Following prior work with similar designs <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Bin Meshar et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Hehman et al., 2018;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Stolier et al., 2018)</ref>, we aimed to collect ratings from ~30 participants per pair.

text.text: To minimize fatigue, each participant was randomly assigned to judge a subset of 118 pairs across 15 counterbalanced subsets, yielding a target sample of 450 participants.
A total of 451 participants were recruited via Amazon Mechanical Turk.
Participants who failed more than two attention checks were excluded (n = 93).
The final sample included 358 participants (Mage = 38.30 years, SDage = 10.31 years; 149 female, 207 male, 1 other, 1 declined to answer; 286 White, 43 Black, 14 Asian, 15 another race).
All primary analyses were replicated with the full sample (N = 451) to ensure robustness, and these exclusions had a negligible impact on the pattern of results.
We used the original full-face versions of the 120 stimuli from Study 1 (60 mental states conveyed by two actors).
Each participant completed a face similarity judgment task followed by a conceptual association task.
On each trial, participants evaluated the similarity between two mental state expressions.
There were 1,770 unique pairwise associations among the 60 mental states.
Each participant was assigned to judge 118 pairs both perceptually and conceptually.
Face Similarity Judgments.

Participants viewed two photos of the same actor conveying the two mental states in a given pair, displayed side by side (e.g., for the pair perplexed and suspicious, participants saw the same actor expressing each state).
Half of the 118 pairs featured the female actor and the other half the male actor, counterbalanced across participants.
Participants rated the similarity of the two facial expressions on a 7-point scale (1 = Not at all similar,7 = Extremely similar).
Presentation order was randomized, and three attention checks were included.
Participants then rated their conceptual associations for the same mental state pairs.
For each pair, participants answered the question "At any given moment, how likely is a person to be [perplexed] and [suspicious]?"
on a 7-point scale (1 = Not at all likely,7 = Extremely likely).
Four attention checks were included.

We first tested whether shared conceptual structure corresponded to shared perceptual structure, and then asked the stronger person-specific question of whether individuals' unique conceptual associations predicted corresponding differences in their own perceptions.
We first examined the correspondence between conceptual associations and perceptual similarity at the group level.
For each measure, we constructed a 60 × 60 similarity matrix averaged across participants: one capturing face similarity judgments and one capturing conceptual associations.

Each cell in the face similarity matrix denotes the average similarity rating of each state pair, while each cell in the conceptual association matrix denotes the average conceptual association between state pairs.

We then assessed the correspondence between the two matrices using representational similarity analysis (RSA; Kriegeskorte, 2008), computing a Spearman rank correlation across the 1,770 unique off-diagonal values.
text.formatted: We then assessed the correspondence between the two matrices using representational similarity analysis (RSA; <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">Kriegeskorte, 2008)</ref>, computing a Spearman rank correlation across the 1,770 unique off-diagonal values.

text.text: Spearman's rank correlation was used to not assume a linear relationship between the two measures (Kriegeskorte, 2008).
text.formatted: Spearman's rank correlation was used to not assume a linear relationship between the two measures <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Kriegeskorte, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: As shown in Figure 3, the results revealed a strong positive correlation between the conceptual association matrix and the face similarity matrix, Spearman's 𝜌(1768) = .513, p < .001; 95% CI = [0.476, 0.549].
text.formatted: As shown in Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_3">3</ref>, the results revealed a strong positive correlation between the conceptual association matrix and the face similarity matrix, Spearman's 𝜌(1768) = .513, p < .001; 95% CI = [0.476, 0.549].

text.text: Thus, as predicted, the more strongly associated participants judged two mental states to be (e.g., perplexed and suspicious), the more similar they perceived the corresponding facial expressions to be.

To distinguish shared conceptual structure from perceivers' idiosyncratic associations, we decomposed each participant's conceptual rating for each mental-state pair into two components: the mean rating for that pair among all other participants (i.e., a leave-one-participant-out group mean) and the participant's deviation from that mean.
We entered both components simultaneously into a linear mixed-effects model predicting face similarity judgments, with random intercepts for participants and mental-state pairs.
Shared conceptual associations strongly predicted perceived facial similarity, b = .716, SE = .029, t = 24.84, p < .001, 95% CI [.660, .773].
text.formatted: Shared conceptual associations strongly predicted perceived facial similarity, b = .716, SE = .029, t = 24.84, p < .001, 95% CI [.660, .773].

text.text: Critically, participants' idiosyncratic departures from this shared conceptual structure also predicted their own face similarity judgments, b = .134, SE = .005, t = 27.89, p < .001, 95% CI [.124, .143].

text.text: Thus, when an individual viewed two mental states as more strongly associated than other people did, that individual also perceived the corresponding facial expressions as more similar.

Conceptual associations corresponded to mental-state perception at both shared and person-specific levels.

States believed to co-occur were perceived as perceptually more similar overall, but critically, participants' idiosyncratic departures from shared conceptual structure predicted corresponding differences in their own perceptual judgments.
Thus, individual differences in conceptual organization were reflected in individual differences in how the same mental states were perceived.
Study 3 tested whether this conceptual-perceptual correspondence extends beyond similarity judgments to the specific errors people make when identifying mental states.
We predicted that stronger conceptual associations would increase the likelihood of confusing one state for another, including at the person-specific level.
We recruited 221 participants from Prolific.
Consistent with previous studies, we aimed for approximately 30 ratings per face stimulus, with oversampling to allow for data cleaning.
The 60 mental states were divided into four subsets, each rated by approximately 50 participants.

Participants who failed more than two attention checks and practice trials combined were excluded (n = 4), resulting in a final sample of 217 participants (Mage = 40.48, SDage = 14.46; 138 females, 73 males, 4 identifying as other, and 2 who declined to answer; 161 White, 31 Black, 10 Asian, 15 other).
We used the same 60 mental states from Studies 1 and 2, each depicted by two actors' faces (one male, one female).
To reduce participant fatigue, stimuli were divided into four subsets of 15 mental states each.
Subsets were created to maximize variability in pairwise conceptual associations.
In other words, each subset contained mental state pairs that varied across the full range of conceptual relatedness, from strongly to weakly associated.
We achieved this by selecting the four subsets that maximized the standard deviation of mean conceptual association values within each subset, using Study 2 data.
Participants began with practice trials designed to familiarize them with the 15 mental states they would judge in the face judgments task.
In each practice trial, participants saw a mental state word from their assigned subset (e.g., confused) and selected the matching word from a list of the 15 mental states they would later judge.
This word-matching task was intended to reinforce familiarity with the assigned stimulus set.
Participants completed 10 practice trials, each randomly drawing from the 15 mental states in their assigned subset.
Face Judgments Task.
The face judgments task consisted of two blocks, one for each target actor.
In each block, 15 face stimuli, one depicting each assigned mental state, were presented one at a time in randomized order.
Thus, participants completed 30 face-judgment trials.
On each trial, participants selected the mental state that best matched the target's mental state experience from a list of their 15 assigned mental states.
Block order was counterbalanced across participants.
Two attention checks were included.
Following the face judgments task, participants completed a conceptual association task similar to the one used in Study 2.
In this task, they rated the conceptual association between all possible pairs of their 15 assigned mental states, resulting in a total of 105 unique trials.
On each trial, participants answered, "At any given moment, how likely is a person to be [perplexed] & [suspicious]?"
text.formatted: On each trial, participants answered, "At any given moment, how likely is a person to be <ref type="bibr">[perplexed] & [suspicious]</ref>?"

text.text: on a 7-point scale (1 = Not at all likely,7 = Extremely likely).
Trial order and the left-right ordering of the two states within each trial were randomized.
Six attention checks were included.
We first tested whether shared conceptual associations predicted which mental states were confused overall.

We then asked whether participants' own conceptual associations predicted their specific errors, including whether idiosyncratic associations explained personspecific confusions beyond the group-level structure.
2 Due to a coding error, one mental-state association was missing from a single subset; that association and its corresponding directional face judgment confusions were excluded from all analyses.
For each face stimulus, we calculated the proportion of participants who selected each mental state as their response.

For example, for a face depicting amusement, 64% of participants correctly identified it as amused, while relaxed, grateful, flirtatious, and sarcastic were selected 11%, 11%, 10%, and 3% of the time, respectively; all remaining states were selected 1% or less.
Proportions summed to 100% for each face.
We then averaged these proportions across the two target actors for each mental state expression.
Each non-correct selection reflected a confusion-a mistaken identification of one mental state as another.
For each of the 15 mental states, we therefore calculated 14 confusion scores representing the degree of confusion with every other state.
We retained the directionality of these confusions: for instance, an amused face was misidentified as grateful 11% of the time, while a grateful face was misidentified as amused 50% of the time.
These were treated as distinct values, resulting in 210 confusion scores per subset (15 mental states × 14 confusion scores).
For conceptual associations, we calculated the average association ratings for each pair of mental states across participants.
Since each conceptual association (e.g., amused and grateful) was assessed in only one direction, we assigned the same value to both directional pairs.
For example, if the association between grateful and amused was rated 5 (on the 7-point scale), this value was used for both grateful-amused and amused-grateful pairs.

Indeed, a stronger conceptual association between a given pair of mental states was associated with a higher likelihood of confusion between the two states, Spearman's 𝜌(836) = .648, p < .001, 95% CI = [0.605, 0.686] (Figure 4).
text.formatted: Indeed, a stronger conceptual association between a given pair of mental states was associated with a higher likelihood of confusion between the two states, Spearman's 𝜌(836) = .648, p < .001, 95% CI = [0.605, 0.686] (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_4">4</ref>).

text.text: Thus, at the group level, mental state pairs believed to be more likely to co-occur were also more likely to be confused in perceptual judgments (e.g., mistaking a grateful face for an amused one, or vice-versa).
We next tested whether perceivers' idiosyncratic conceptual associations predicted the specific errors they made beyond shared conceptual structure.
As in Study 2, each participant's conceptual rating for a given state pair was decomposed into the leave-one-participant-out group mean for that pair and the participant's deviation from that mean.

Because each face judgment involved a mutually exclusive choice among response labels, we restricted this analysis to trials on which a participant made an error and fit a conditional logistic regression predicting which incorrect label was selected from these shared and idiosyncratic conceptual components, conditioning on each face-judgment trial and clustering standard errors by participant.
Shared conceptual associations strongly predicted which incorrect state was selected, b = .968, SE = .030, z = 31.84, p < .001, OR = 2.632, 95% CI [2.480, 2.794].
text.formatted: Shared conceptual associations strongly predicted which incorrect state was selected, b = .968, SE = .030, z = 31.84, p < .001, OR = 2.632, 95% CI [2.480, 2.794].

text.text: Critically, participants' idiosyncratic conceptual associations also predicted their specific confusions, b = .061, SE = .016, z = 3.73, p < .001, OR = 1.063, 95% CI [1.029, 1.097], see figure 4.
text.formatted: Critically, participants' idiosyncratic conceptual associations also predicted their specific confusions, b = .061, SE = .016, z = 3.73, p < .001, OR = 1.063, 95% CI [1.029, 1.097], see figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_4">4</ref>.

text.text: Thus, given that a participant misidentified a face, they were more likely to select a particular incorrect state when they personally viewed that state as more strongly associated with the depicted state than other participants did.
Conceptual associations predicted specific mental-state confusions at both shared and person-specific levels.

Mental state pairs believed to be more likely to co-occur were more frequently confused in face judgments, and participants were more likely to select a particular incorrect state when they viewed it as more strongly associated with the depicted state, even after accounting for shared associations.

Study 3 showed that conceptual structure predicts not only perceived similarity but the specific mental states perceivers confuse, including errors explained by perceivers' idiosyncratic conceptual associations.

Study 4 asked whether this correspondence generalizes to naturalistic faces, where facial appearance and expression vary substantially across individuals rather than being constrained by two actors' standardized poses.
As in Study 3, we aimed to recruit at least 30 participants per stimulus and oversampled to account for data cleaning.
Because the study included two versions with different stimuli, we recruited a total of 102 participants through Prolific.
No participants met our exclusion criteria of failing more than two practice trials and/or attention checks (Mage = 43.07, SDage = 12.92; 62 females, 40 males; 73 White, 18 Black, 7 Asian, 4 other).
We sought a larger, more naturalistic set of face stimuli than those used in Studies 1-3.

We selected stimuli from Cowen and Keltner (2020), a dataset of 1,500 ambient, naturally occurring faces crowdsourced from millions of individuals worldwide (rather than explicitly posed by actors), each rated by independent raters on 28 emotional states.
text.formatted: We selected stimuli from <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Cowen and Keltner (2020)</ref>, a dataset of 1,500 ambient, naturally occurring faces crowdsourced from millions of individuals worldwide (rather than explicitly posed by actors), each rated by independent raters on 28 emotional states.

text.text: We selected faces for which raters agreed that one emotional state was present at 50% intensity or higher, treating that state as the face's perceived primary state.
Out of the 28 states in the original dataset, 15 had at least 10 face stimuli meeting this threshold.
A complete list of selected stimuli is available on OSF.
For each of the 15 states, we selected the 10 faces with the highest intensity ratings.
When multiple stimuli shared similar intensity values, we prioritized those with the highest image resolution, then selected randomly among remaining ties.
This yielded 150 stimuli in total (15 states × 10 faces each).
Because this set was too large for a single session, we randomly divided the stimuli into two subsets of 75 faces (five per state), and participants were assigned to one version.
This heterogeneity allowed us to test whether conceptual associations predict confusion patterns despite substantial variation in facial appearance and expression.
As in Study 3, participants categorized each face using 15 possible mental state response options.
The procedure was identical to Study 3, with the only difference being the stimuli evaluated.

As in Study 3, we tested whether conceptual associations predicted perceptual confusions at both shared and person-specific levels, including whether individuals' unique associations predicted their own errors beyond the group-level structure.

Using the same analytic approach as Study 3, we replicated the strong positive association between conceptual associations and patterns of perceptual confusion at the group level, this time with unposed naturalistic faces, Spearman's 𝜌(208) = .572, p < .001, 95% CI = [0.476, 0.656] (Figure 4).
text.formatted: Using the same analytic approach as Study 3, we replicated the strong positive association between conceptual associations and patterns of perceptual confusion at the group level, this time with unposed naturalistic faces, Spearman's 𝜌(208) = .572, p < .001, 95% CI = [0.476, 0.656] (Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_4">4</ref>).

text.text: When two states were more conceptually related, participants were more likely to confuse those states when judging naturalistic facial expressions.
For example, if amusement is believed to co-occur with surprise, then perceivers were more likely to confuse these two states in naturalistic, self-evoked facial expressions.
At the individual level, we again decomposed conceptual associations into the leave-oneparticipant-out group mean for each state pair and each participant's idiosyncratic deviation from that mean.

We then used the same conditional-choice analysis as in Study 3, restricting the analysis to erroneous face judgments and predicting which incorrect state was selected while conditioning on each face-judgment trial and clustering standard errors by participant.
Shared conceptual associations strongly predicted which incorrect state participants selected, b = .732, SE = .039, z = 18.78, p < .001, OR = 2.080, 95% CI [1.927, 2.245].
text.formatted: Shared conceptual associations strongly predicted which incorrect state participants selected, b = .732, SE = .039, z = 18.78, p < .001, OR = 2.080, 95% <ref type="bibr">CI [1.927,</ref> <ref type="bibr">2.245]</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, participants' idiosyncratic conceptual associations also predicted their specific errors, b = .054, SE = .025, z = 2.19, p = .028, OR = 1.056, 95% CI [1.006, 1.109], see Figure 4.
text.formatted: Importantly, participants' idiosyncratic conceptual associations also predicted their specific errors, b = .054, SE = .025, z = 2.19, p = .028, OR = 1.056, 95% CI [1.006, 1.109], see Figure <ref type="figure" target="#fig_4">4</ref>.

text.text: Thus, even for naturalistic, unposed faces, participants were more likely to make a particular confusion when they personally viewed the depicted and selected states as more strongly associated than other participants did.

Study 4 replicated the correspondence between conceptual structure and mental-state confusions across naturalistic faces, including at the person-specific level after accounting for shared associations.
Thus, the relationship generalized beyond standardized posed expressions despite substantial variation in facial appearance and expression.

Across four studies, mental state judgments reflected information distributed across the face as well as perceivers' conceptual associations among mental states.
In Study 1, participants were more accurate in identifying mental states from full faces than from partial faces or isolated eye regions.

While prior work has emphasized the eyes as the primary window into others' mental states (e.g., Baron-Cohen et al., 2001; Lee & Anderson, 2017; Looser & Wheatley, 2010), our findings show that inferences of complex mental states consistently rely on more than the eye region alone.
text.formatted: While prior work has emphasized the eyes as the primary window into others' mental states (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">Baron-Cohen et al., 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Lee & Anderson, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Looser & Wheatley, 2010)</ref>, our findings show that inferences of complex mental states consistently rely on more than the eye region alone.

text.text: In fact, excluding the eyes permitted more accurate judgments than presenting them in isolation, suggesting that regions like the mouth carry substantial expressive information for complex mental state attributions.
Few studies have challenged the notion that the eyes play a privileged role in communicating mental states.

Prior research has found that the most diagnostic facial region varies by mental state: while some states rely more heavily on the eyes, others draw on the mouth or on coordinated movements across regions (Back et al., 2009; Blais et al., 2012; Yuki et al., 2007; Jack et al., 2012).
text.formatted: Prior research has found that the most diagnostic facial region varies by mental state: while some states rely more heavily on the eyes, others draw on the mouth or on coordinated movements across regions <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Back et al., 2009;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Blais et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b39">Yuki et al., 2007;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Jack et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: However, this prior research examined basic emotion expressions or a small number of mental states, leaving open whether the importance of non-eye cues extends to the broader range of complex, nuanced states people infer in daily life.

The present research demonstrates that across 60 distinct mental states, perceivers rely heavily on cues beyond the eyes, often more so than on the eyes themselves, suggesting that mental state communication depends on a richer constellation of facial information than previously recognized.
In Study 2, we showed that beyond bottom-up facial cues, top-down conceptual associations were also systematically related to mental state perception at both shared and person-specific levels.

Mental states that were more strongly associated in the mind were perceived as more visually similar, but importantly, participants' idiosyncratic departures from the group's conceptual structure also predicted their own perceptual judgments.

Studies 3 and 4 extended this relationship to specific mental state confusions: participants were more likely to misidentify a depicted state as another state when the two were more strongly conceptually associated.
This pattern emerged across both posed and naturalistic expressions, suggesting a robust correspondence between conceptual structure and mental state inference.

A growing body of research has shown that conceptual knowledge plays a central role in social categorization, trait attribution, and emotion recognition (e.g., Bin Meshar et al., 2022; Brooks et al., 2019; Freeman et al., 2020; Stolier et al., 2018).
text.formatted: A growing body of research has shown that conceptual knowledge plays a central role in social categorization, trait attribution, and emotion recognition (e.g., Bin <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Meshar et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">Brooks et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Freeman et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Stolier et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Our findings extend this work by demonstrating that both shared and idiosyncratic conceptual structures correspond to how perceivers represent mental states in faces and which states they confuse with one another.
While conceptual associations may help scaffold interpretations of complex facial expressions, they may also direct inferences toward related but incorrect mental states.
This pattern suggests that more differentiated conceptual representations (i.e., deeming two states as less likely to co-occur) may reduce confusion between them in faces.

This is consistent with research on emotional granularity, which links finer-grained emotion representations to more accurate recognition of others' emotional experiences (Israelashvili et al., 2019), greater empathic accuracy, and more effective social support (Erbas et al., 2016; Gregory et al., 2020).
text.formatted: This is consistent with research on emotional granularity, which links finer-grained emotion representations to more accurate recognition of others' emotional experiences <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Israelashvili et al., 2019)</ref>, greater empathic accuracy, and more effective social support <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Erbas et al., 2016;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Gregory et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: This work is not without limitations.
Our findings are correlational and do not establish that conceptual knowledge causally alters perception.
Conceptual associations may themselves reflect experienced patterns and transitions between mental states (Thornton et al., 2023), creating bidirectional influence.
text.formatted: Conceptual associations may themselves reflect experienced patterns and transitions between mental states <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Thornton et al., 2023)</ref>, creating bidirectional influence.

text.text: Although the person-specific effects make a purely shared stimulus explanation less likely, they do not resolve causal direction.
Future work should manipulate conceptual knowledge directly to test its causal impact on mental-state inference.
In sum, mental-state inference draws on information distributed across the face and the conceptual structure through which perceivers interpret it.
Beyond showing that the eyes are not uniquely privileged, our findings reveal that shared and person-specific conceptual associations correspond to which states look alike and which are confused.
Conceptual knowledge may therefore explain not only commonalities in how people perceive others' minds, but systematic differences between perceivers confronted with the same social information.
Understanding others is not merely a matter of reading faces, but of reading them through a structured model of how mental states relate.
We expect these findings to generalize mostly to mental state judgments from static facial images.
Whether these findings extend to dynamic facial expressions remains unknown.
In addition, our primary stimuli featured two White young-adult actors posing 60 mental states, which afforded precision and control but limited generalizability.
Study 4 partially addressed this by using a more diverse, naturalistic stimulus set.

However, systematic comparisons across race, age, and other sociodemographic variables will be important, given that these attributes likely affect mental-state perception through stereotype-based conceptual associations (Freeman & Lin, 2025).

text.text: Across four studies, we test a more comprehensive account of how facial cues and conceptual knowledge shape mental-state perception.
Study 1 examines whether full facial cues, compared to the eye region alone or all features excluding the eyes, lead to higher inference accuracy across 60 unique mental states.
Study 2 tests whether shared and person-specific conceptual associations predict corresponding similarities in perceived facial expressions.
Study 3 then examines whether conceptual associations predict specific perceptual confusions between mental states.
Finally, Study 4 tests whether these confusion patterns generalize to naturalistic, unposed expressions.
